name: Cinnamon (stick)
notes: Cassia is hotter than Ceylon; one 3–4 g stick per gallon (~1 g/L) is already clearly present.

name: Vanilla bean
notes: One bean ≈ 3–4 g. Smooths acidity and alcohol heat.

name: Clove
notes: Extremely potent (eugenol). 1 clove ≈ 0.1 g; 2–3 per 5 gallons is plenty.

name: Nutmeg
notes: Turns soapy/medicinal fast — err low.

name: Allspice
notes: Clove-like; reduce clove if combining.

name: Star anise
notes: Pod ≈ 0.5 g; licorice dominates quickly.

name: Cardamom (green)
notes: Bright, eucalyptus-citrus; pairs with orange blossom honey and pear.

name: Ginger (fresh)
notes: Fresh root; dried powder is ~5× stronger by weight.

name: Black pepper
notes: Adds perceived dryness and heat.

name: Oak cubes (medium toast)
notes: Chips extract in ~2 weeks, cubes in 2–3 months. Adds tannin and vanillin.

name: Lavender (dried)
notes: Soapy above ~0.3 g/L. Taste daily.

name: Chamomile (dried)
notes: Apple-floral; good with light honey.

name: Hibiscus (dried)
notes: Adds colour and lots of acid — lowers pH.

name: Rose petals (dried)
notes: Rhodomel; perfumed — balance with acidity.

name: Orange zest
notes: Pith adds bitterness — zest only.

name: Coffee (whole beans)
notes: Cold-steep in secondary; extracts in 24–72 h.

name: Cacao nibs
notes: Soak in vodka first to sanitise; pairs with cherry and vanilla.

name: Chili (jalapeño, fresh)
notes: Capsicumel. Heat builds fast; taste every 12–24 h.

name: Lemongrass
notes: Bright citrus without acid.

name: Elderflower (dried)
notes: Lychee-muscat perfume; classic with gooseberry, pear and light honey. Florets only — stems are bitter.

name: Meadowsweet (dried)
notes: Historic 'mead-wort': almond-honey, wintergreen. Strong above ~1 g/L.

name: Orange blossom (dried)
notes: Neroli perfume; amplifies orange-blossom honey.

name: Jasmine (dried)
notes: Heady and indolic; turns perfumey quickly.

name: Butterfly pea flower
notes: Mostly colour, little flavour. Blue at high pH, violet-pink in acidic mead: a fun colour-change show.

name: Linden / lime blossom (dried)
notes: Honeyed, soft floral; very mead-friendly.

name: Calendula (dried)
notes: Golden colour, gentle resinous note.

name: Rosehip (dried)
notes: Tart, tea-like; adds acidity and orange-red colour.

name: Heather tips (dried)
notes: Traditional Scottish brewing herb; floral-bitter.

name: Mint (fresh)
notes: Fades fast in the bottle; add late.

name: Thyme (fresh)
notes: Savoury-floral; lovely with lemon and wildflower honey.

name: American oak chips (medium toast)
notes: Fast: chips give most of their flavour in 1–2 weeks. American oak is sweeter, with more vanilla and coconut than French.

name: French oak chips (medium toast)
notes: Finer grain than American oak: spicier and more restrained, with silkier tannin.

name: French oak cubes (medium+ toast)
notes: Slow and layered: cubes need 4–12 weeks. About 3.7 g/L (3 oz per 6 gal) is a common full dose.

name: Hungarian oak cubes (medium+ toast)
notes: Between French and American in character; good with dark fruit and spiced meads.

name: American oak cubes (heavy toast)
notes: Heavy toast trades fresh-wood tannin for caramel, coffee and smoke. Great in sack and dessert meads.

name: Bourbon barrel chips
notes: Charred American oak from used bourbon barrels: brings whiskey character as well as oak.

name: Rum barrel chips
notes: Used rum-barrel oak: molasses and tropical spice. Pairs with pineapple, banana and baking spice.

name: Red wine barrel chips
notes: Wine-soaked oak: red fruit and soft tannin. Suits berry melomels and pyments.

name: Acacia wood chips (light toast)
notes: Low in tannin, adds a honeyed, floral note without masking the varietal. A natural fit for traditional meads.

name: Cherry wood chips
notes: Sweet, nutty wood that works with cherry and stone fruit. Taste early: it turns bitter if overdone.

name: Chestnut tannin (powder)
use: Dissolve in a little warm water, stir in and wait a week before judging. Bench-trial first: tannin cannot be taken out.
notes: Hydrolysable tannin from sweet-chestnut wood: a firm, slightly sweet grip that also protects colour and aroma from oxygen. Products are dosed 5–20 g/hL (0.05–0.2 g/L) in mead; up to ~0.5 g/L in primary as a fermentation tannin.

name: Grape (wine) tannin powder
use: Dissolve in a little warm water, stir in and wait a week before judging. Bench-trial first.
notes: Condensed tannin from grape skins and seeds: softer and fruitier than wood tannins. The classic fix for a flat or cloying mead.

name: Oak tannin powder
use: Dissolve in a little warm water, stir in and wait a week before judging. Bench-trial first.
notes: Ellagic tannin extracted from oak: oak-like structure without the wood. Strong, so doses are low.

name: L-phenylalanine
use: Dissolve in a little must and add at pitch: the yeast converts it during fermentation.
notes: An amino acid the yeast turns into 2-phenylethanol (rose and honey aroma) during fermentation; it is not tasted directly. Mead makers use 0.14–0.28 g/L. It carries a little nitrogen but is a poor nitrogen source, so the nutrient plan ignores it.

name: Toasted coconut
notes: Toast unsweetened flakes until golden. Fat floats: rack carefully off any oily film.

name: Hops (dry-hop pellets)
notes: For hopped meads: dry-hop for 3–7 days after fermentation. Citrusy varieties (Citra, Mosaic) suit hydromels; noble hops suit traditionals.

name: Pectic enzyme (pectinase)
use: Add with the fruit, ideally 12 h before the yeast. Doses vary by brand: follow the label.
notes: Breaks down fruit pectin: more juice, less haze. Not a flavour. Powder is often ½ tsp per gallon (~0.3 g/L).

name: Bentonite (clay fining)
use: Hydrate in 10× its weight of hot water for 24 h, stir in, then rack off after 1–2 weeks.
notes: Clay that drops proteins and haze. Strips a little aroma at high doses, so use only what clears it.

name: Yeast hulls (ghosts)
use: Add at the start of a high-gravity ferment, or to rescue a stuck one.
notes: Yeast cell walls that soak up toxic fatty acids and give the yeast a surface to work on. Not a flavour.
